questions.prompt: The booking conditions of an agency read: "A deposit of 20 % is payable on booking. The deposit is not refundable less than thirty days before departure." Karim booked in June, paid the deposit, then cancelled ten days before his flight. What happens to his deposit?

options.text: he gets it back in full, since he cancelled
it is turned into a discount on his next booking
he owes the balance of the price as well
he loses it: the agency is entitled to keep it

questions.explanation: The small print says two things and both of them bite here. A deposit is payable on booking, and it stops being refundable once the deadline printed in the conditions has passed. Karim cancelled ten days before departure, well inside the thirty-day limit, so the agency keeps the money. Getting it back in full is what would have happened before that date; a deposit is not converted into a discount on a future trip, which would be a favour and not a right; and a cancelled booking leaves no balance to pay.

questions.prompt: A guest writes to the hotel: "You said that we will be met at the airport, but nobody was there." One word in her report has not stepped back into the past, although it should have. Which one?

options.text: will
said
met
was

questions.explanation: After a reporting verb in the past, will steps back to would: you said that we would be met at the airport. Will belongs to the moment when the promise was made, in front of a customer who had not travelled yet, and leaving it standing in the report is the commonest mistake of the whole lesson. The reporting verb is already in the past, the past participle inside the passive never moves, and the last verb is the guest's own account of what really happened.

questions.prompt: A customer is complaining at the agency desk. Match each of her sentences with the move it makes in her complaint.

options.text: I'm afraid I have to make a complaint about last week's trip.
Our room had no balcony and looked onto the kitchens.
Your brochure promised a balcony over the gardens.
I'd like the difference between the two rooms refunded.
recalling the promise that was broken
opening the complaint and naming its subject
saying what she wants from the agency
stating the facts of what she found in the room

questions.explanation: A complaint that carries makes four moves in this order. You open it by announcing that it is a complaint and naming its subject, so that nobody has to guess why you are there. You give the facts, plainly, so that nobody has to take your word for them. You bring back the promise that was broken, which is the move that usually calls for reported speech — though naming a promise, as she does here, binds the agency quite as firmly as quoting it. And you finish with a request that fits: the difference between the room she paid for and the room she was given, and not the whole week's bill.

questions.prompt: You are at the hotel desk. Your room had no hot water for three nights and you want the manager to act. Which sentence complains firmly but politely?

options.text: Whoever runs your maintenance here has no idea what he is doing.
I don't want to make a fuss about it, so please don't trouble yourself.
We had no hot water for three nights, and I'd like that put right.
Would you call three cold nights acceptable in a four-star hotel?

questions.explanation: Firmness goes at the fault; rudeness goes at the people. Naming what went wrong, saying how long it lasted and asking for it to be put right keeps the conversation where you need it, on the water. Blaming whoever runs the maintenance invites the manager to defend his staff instead of heating it. Promising not to make a fuss tells him that nothing need be done. And asking whether three cold nights are acceptable is not really a question: it scores a point and changes nothing.

questions.prompt: Say the word "disappointed" aloud. Which line shows where its main stress falls?

options.text: DIS-ap-point-ed
dis-ap-POINT-ed
dis-AP-point-ed
dis-ap-point-ED

questions.explanation: Disappointed has four syllables and the third is the one you push hardest: dis-ap-POINT-ed. It is the syllable that carries the meaning of the word, the one you also hear stressed in appoint. English gives a long word exactly one main stress, never two, and the ending -ed of an adjective is never the syllable that takes it.

questions.prompt: At the counter. Customer: "Are the airport taxes included in that price?" Agent: "They are, madam, but the excursions aren't." The customer books the package holiday. What will she still have to pay for once she is there?

options.text: the taxes at the airport
the transfer from the airport
the breakfast at the hotel
the excursions she goes on

questions.explanation: The agent's answer does two jobs in one line: it confirms one thing and excludes another. The taxes are covered by the price she is about to pay, while the excursions are not, so each of them will be paid for on the spot, on the day she goes on it. The other two are what a package normally carries already, the ride in from the airport and the first meal of the day, so paying for either of them again would be paying twice. Listen for the word that excludes: it marks the only place where her money will still be needed.
